title: Serving API and Compatibility Contracts
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to define a provider-neutral serving API contract and evaluate whether a proposed change preserves behavior expected by existing clients. After completing it, learners can identify request, response, and error changes that require compatibility testing.
objectives: Describe a serving API contract in terms of observable request, response, and error behavior.
Classify a proposed API change as compatible, incompatible, or requiring additional evidence.
Design compatibility checks that exercise interactions accepted by the existing contract.
Explain how a change in meaning can break compatibility even when the data shape remains unchanged.

sections.title: Source update
paragraphs: The prior citation entry named content/modules/self-hosted-model-operations/serving-api-and-compatibility-contracts.json was an unregistered local path and had never been verified. It was not retained as a source because it is not a directly resolvable HTTPS reference.

That citation has been replaced by the RFC Editor documents for HTTP semantics and HTTP API problem details. The correction affects the attribution supporting this module's descriptions of request and response semantics and structured error responses. Provider-specific and implementation-specific claims unsupported by those sources are omitted.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that the learner can already recognize an API request, an API response, headers, and a structured message body. It does not assume knowledge of any particular provider, serving product, deployment system, or client library.
The focus is the compatibility boundary visible to a client. Internal server organization is outside that boundary unless it changes an observable request, response, or error.

sections.title: Define the observable contract
paragraphs: An HTTP serving contract should identify the request method, target, representation metadata, body meaning, response status, response metadata, response-body meaning, and error behavior that a client may rely on. HTTP Semantics defines the roles of methods, status codes, fields, and message content in an HTTP interaction.

A useful contract states both structure and meaning. Structure describes what a client sends or receives. Meaning describes how the server interprets a request and what a response communicates. Preserving structure while changing meaning does not preserve the same contract.

Write requirements from the client's perspective. For each accepted request, state what makes it valid, which parts are optional, and what response categories the client must be prepared to handle. For each response, state which information is guaranteed and which information may vary.

sections.title: Reason about compatibility
paragraphs: Evaluate a proposed change against interactions permitted by the existing contract. First ask whether a request that was previously valid is still accepted with the same meaning. Then ask whether an existing client can interpret the resulting response without changing the meaning it observes. Finally, apply the same questions to error responses.

A change is incompatible when it invalidates behavior that the existing contract allowed or alters a guarantee on which an existing client may rely. Examples include rejecting a previously valid request, removing guaranteed response information, or assigning a different meaning to an existing value.

A change cannot be declared compatible merely because one example succeeds. Compatibility evidence should cover representative valid requests, boundary cases described by the contract, successful responses, and documented error paths. If the existing contract does not establish how clients handle a proposed addition, the compatibility result requires additional evidence rather than an assumption.

sections.title: Keep error behavior within the contract
paragraphs: Errors are part of the client-visible contract. A client may depend on the response status, the representation metadata, and stable machine-readable information in the response body.

Problem Details for HTTP APIs defines a structured format for communicating machine-readable details about an HTTP API problem. When a contract adopts such a format, compatibility review must consider both the HTTP response and the documented meaning of the structured problem information.

Changing an error from one documented meaning to another can affect retry logic, user messages, or corrective client behavior even if the response body remains syntactically valid. Error-path tests should therefore assert meaning as well as parseability.

sections.title: Build a compatibility check
paragraphs: Start with examples that are valid under the existing contract. Submit those interactions to the proposed implementation and compare the observable results with the original guarantees. Check acceptance, response category, required information, and documented meaning.

Separate a parse check from a semantic check. A parse check asks whether the client can read the response. A semantic check asks whether the response still communicates what the contract promised. Passing only the parse check is insufficient when a field or error has changed meaning.
Record the contract rule exercised by each check. This makes a failure traceable to a specific compatibility promise and prevents an implementation detail from being mistaken for a public guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which information belongs in the client-visible serving API contract described in this module?
choices: Only the server's internal component layout
Request, response, and error behavior observable by a client
Only whether the response body can be parsed
questions.explanation: The module defines the compatibility boundary through observable request, response, and error behavior. Internal organization is outside that boundary unless it changes observable behavior.

questions.prompt: A response keeps the same data shape, but an existing value is assigned a different documented meaning. How should that change be evaluated?
choices: It is automatically compatible because the shape is unchanged
It is irrelevant because clients only observe syntax
It is incompatible when it alters a guarantee on which an existing client may rely
It requires no testing if the response can be parsed
questions.explanation: The module states that preserving structure while changing meaning does not preserve the same contract. Changing a documented meaning can alter a client-visible guarantee.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate starting point for a compatibility check?
choices: Interactions that are valid under the existing contract
Only newly invented requests that the old contract did not permit
The proposed server's internal source layout
A single successful parse with no semantic assertions
questions.explanation: The module instructs learners to start with interactions valid under the existing contract and compare their observable results with the original guarantees.

questions.prompt: What did the source correction in this update affect?
choices: It changed the module to an advanced level
It replaced an unverified local citation and corrected attribution for HTTP semantics and structured error behavior
It introduced claims about an unnamed deployment product
questions.explanation: The source-update section states that the unverified local path was replaced by resolvable RFC Editor sources supporting request, response, and structured error descriptions.
